540.title: He made Himself
540.hook: He created Himself, then the Name, then the world, and sat watching it with delight (Asa di Var 1, ang 463)
540.howItsDone: The first pauri of Asa di Var, sung each morning in gurdwaras, describes God as self-made, taking on the Name, making the world, and sitting within it to watch with delight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chaanan: a hundred moons can't light the inside; the guru is the light. Today, the first pauri, the first rung of the ballad.

A potter finishes a bowl, sets it on the shelf, and steps back. A gardener stands at the edge of a bed she planted in spring, now full of tomatoes. A father watches his daughter take her first wobbly steps across the kitchen. There's a look on a maker's face in that moment, half pride and half wonder, as if they can't quite believe it's real. The first pauri of Asa di Var says God has that look too.
screen: `A POTTER STEPS BACK.` → `A GARDEN FULL OF TOMATOES.` → `THE LOOK ON A MAKER'S FACE.`

segments.voice: The first pauri begins, in paraphrase: He Himself fashioned Himself, and Himself took on the Name. Second, He made the creation, and seated within it, He watches it with delight. Then it turns to praise: You are the Giver and the Maker; pleased, You give and bless. You know everyone; You give life and can take it back with a word. Take the order slowly. First, aapeenai aap saajio: He made Himself. Nobody made God. God is self-existent, the same idea Sikhs recite every day in the Mool Mantar as saibhang. Second, the Name: God takes on naau, which in Gurbani means God made known, God expressed. Only then the world, kudrat, the creation. Then the lovely part: kar aasan, having taken a seat, ditho chaau, He watched with delight. Aasan is a seat, the cushion or mat you sit on. God doesn't make the world and leave, like a builder handing over keys. God sits down inside it. And chaau is delight, eagerness, the joy of a festival or a wedding. So the God of this first pauri isn't a distant engineer or a grim judge. It's a maker who sits down in the middle of the work and enjoys it. That says something about the world, too. If its Maker watches it with delight, it's worth delighting in: tomatoes, first steps, the bowl on the shelf. Before Asa di Var gets sharp about pride and pretending, as it will, it sets this down first: a world made with joy.

segments.voice: Picture something you made, a meal, a garden, a letter, a friendship you tended, and sit with it the way the pauri says God sits with creation. Not judging the flaws; just watching, with delight. If you pray, rest in Waheguru, the Maker who watches with delight.
Chaau, delight or eagerness: Asa di Var's first pauri says God made Himself, then the Name, then the world, and took a seat within it, watching with chaau.
Your line: watching with delight. The Maker never left the workshop. Day five hundred forty, done.

541.title: The salok of wonder
541.hook: wonder is the sound, wonder the scripture, wonder the creatures, wonder the colors (Asa di Var, ang 463)
541.howItsDone: Asa di Var's salok of wonder, sung each morning in gurdwaras, repeats vismaad line after line, and Sikhs hear the same awe in waah, the opening of Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chaau: the Maker sat down inside creation and watched it with delight. Today Guru Nanak looks at that same creation and can't stop saying one word.

Watch a toddler meet a dog for the first time. The eyes go wide. The mouth opens. Sometimes there's a long whoa, sometimes just a small body gone still with astonishment. Then the child points and looks at you: are you seeing this? Somewhere along the way, grown-ups stop making that face. We've seen dogs. We've seen rain. Guru Nanak, in Asa di Var, writes a salok that sounds like that toddler's whoa, over and over.
screen: `A TODDLER MEETS A DOG.` → `EYES WIDE, A LONG WHOA.` → `ARE YOU SEEING THIS?`

segments.voice: The salok begins almost every phrase with one word: vismaad. Wonder, awe, astonishment. In paraphrase, it runs like this. Wonder is the sound, wonder is the sacred knowledge. Wonder are the living beings, wonder their many kinds. Wonder are the forms, wonder the colors. Wonder, creatures wandering about unclothed. Wonder is the wind, wonder the water, wonder the fire that plays its marvels. Wonder the earth, wonder the sources of life. Wonder, union; wonder, parting. Wonder, hunger; wonder, being fed. Wonder near, wonder far. It keeps going, line after line, like a drumbeat. Notice what Guru Nanak puts on the list. Not only lovely things. Parting is there, and hunger, and the wilderness alongside the path. Vismaad isn't a sunset filter laid over the hard parts of life. It's astonishment at all of it, the strange, enormous fact that anything exists at all. Then the ending, in paraphrase: seeing these marvels, I am struck with wonder. Nanak says, to understand this comes by perfect good fortune. In Sikh teaching, vismaad is more than a feeling. It's a spiritual state: the place where cleverness runs out and only awe is left. Sikh tradition hears the same awe in the name Waheguru, which opens with waah, the Punjabi cry of wonder. The toddler's whoa is not so far from prayer.

segments.voice: Look out a window, or picture the last time you were outdoors, and wait until something catches you: a cloud, a weed in a crack, a bird. Stay with it and let it be astonishing, then find a second wonder, and a third. If you pray, whisper Waheguru at each one.

542.title: All is His power
542.hook: by His power we see and hear, by His power fear and joy (Asa di Var, ang 464)
542.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the gurdwara at dawn, and the word kudrat is common in everyday Punjabi for nature and the created world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vismaad: wonder at all of it, even hunger and parting. Today the very next salok gives that wonder a name.

Hold your hand up to a window and look at it. The skin, the lines across the palm, the faint pulse at the wrist. You didn't design any of it. You didn't decide to have eyes that could see it, or a brain that could wonder about it. Yesterday Guru Nanak stood in front of creation and could only say wonder. Today, in the salok right after, he names the force running through every piece. One word, returning in nearly every line: kudrat.
screen: `LOOK AT YOUR OWN HAND.` → `YOU DIDN'T DESIGN ANY OF IT.` → `ONE WORD, IN NEARLY EVERY LINE.`

segments.voice: Kudrat is a word Punjabi shares with Persian and Arabic. It means power, the power to make and to do, and in everyday Punjabi it also came to mean nature, the created world itself. Both meanings hum in this salok, on ang 464. Guru Nanak begins with the senses. By your power we see, by your power we hear. By your power there is fear, and there is joy, the very core of happiness. Then the list widens. Your power is in the worlds below and the skies above, in every form. It's in the scriptures, he says, naming the Vedas and Puranas and the Semitic books alike. It's in eating and drinking and getting dressed. It's in love. It's in every species and color, in air and water and fire, in the dust of the earth. And then a line that can surprise. Your power is in good deeds, and in bad ones. Honor and pride, too. Guru Nanak doesn't keep a clean list of pleasant things. Everything that happens, happens inside this one power. The salok ends by turning to the One: all is your kudrat, and you are kaadir, the powerful Creator. Kaadir and kudrat sound alike, almost a signature: the power and the Powerful belong together. The last line says Nanak sees the One at work within the hukam, the divine order, utterly alone and beyond all. So the point isn't fear of a strong God. It's attention. If power is in the seeing, your next glance is part of it. If it's in the eating, lunch is part of it. A Sikh walking through an ordinary day, the salok suggests, never leaves the creation's workshop.
screen: `KUDRAT: POWER, AND NATURE.` · `IN SEEING, HEARING, FEAR AND JOY.` · `IN GOOD DEEDS AND IN BAD.` · `KUDRAT AND KAADIR SOUND ALIKE.` · then, large: `ALL IS YOUR POWER.`

segments.voice: Look at a single leaf, real or remembered, and follow one vein from stem to edge. Inside it, right now, light is becoming food and water is rising, with no one's help; then look at your own hand and notice the same quiet work. If you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.
Kudrat. Power, and the creation that power makes. In Guru Nanak's salok, it runs through seeing, hearing, eating, loving, and every color on earth.
Your line: his power. It's in the seeing, so it's in this moment too. See you tomorrow.

543.title: In awe the wind blows
543.hook: in awe the wind blows and rivers run; only the Formless is without fear (Asa di Var, ang 464)
543.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of awe in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many know its refrain, bhai vich, in awe, from long listening in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kudrat: power and nature in one word, running through all of it. Today a salok a little further on shows the whole creation moving in awe.

Every morning the sun comes up within a few minutes of when the tables say it will. Tides arrive on schedule. Rivers that ran downhill in your grandparents' time still run downhill. Nobody stands on the mountain telling the water where to go. Scientists call these patterns laws. Guru Nanak, looking at the same faithful river and punctual sun, reached for a word you might not expect. Not law. Bhau. Fear, or awe. And in one long salok he hears the entire universe living inside it.
screen: `THE SUN, ON SCHEDULE.` → `RIVERS STILL RUN DOWNHILL.` → `GURU NANAK'S WORD: BHAU.`

segments.voice: Bhau is the Punjabi word at the center of this salok on ang 464, and it's hard to put into English. It can mean fear. But in Gurbani it often means something closer to reverence: the trembling respect of someone at the edge of a canyon. Listen to how the salok builds. Bhai vich, in awe, the wind blows, always. In awe a hundred thousand rivers flow. In awe fire does its work. In awe the earth carries its load. In awe Indra, lord of the rains, goes about head-down. In awe the sun and the moon travel their endless miles. In awe stand the adepts and the gods, the warriors and the mighty heroes, and in awe the crowds of people come and go. Notice the pictures. Wind that never takes a day off. Rivers that never refuse. Fire that keeps burning as if under orders. Guru Nanak is describing faithfulness. Everything in creation keeps its place and does its job, because it moves within the One's hukam, the divine order. Bhau is what that looks like from the inside. Then the turn. Awe, the salok says, is written on every forehead: sun, river, god, warrior. Only one is without fear: the Formless, the One who is true. Tomorrow we stay with that line. For today, one thing. In Sikh teaching, this awe isn't meant to make a person small and frightened. Elsewhere Gurbani pairs bhau with bhaau, awe with love, and some Sikh teachers describe the right kind of awe as what keeps love honest. The wind doesn't blow out of terror. It blows because it knows where it belongs.

segments.voice: Feel the air on your face, or your own breath, the small wind you carry everywhere, moving without being asked. This air has moved faithfully since long before you and will move long after; let a little of the salok's awe settle in. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Bhau, awe or fear: Guru Nanak's picture of a faithful creation, wind, rivers, fire, earth, sun and moon, all moving bhai vich, in awe, within the One's order.
Your line: everything in awe. The wind knows where it belongs. Day five hundred forty-three, done.

544.title: The fearless Formless
544.hook: Nanak says the Formless alone is fearless; all else is dust by comparison (Asa di Var, ang 464)
544.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the word nirbhau every day in the Mool Mantar, and hear this salok on the fearless Formless when Asa di Var is sung at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhau: wind, rivers, sun and kings, all moving in awe. And one alone without fear. Today we stand with that one line.

If you've been on this path since the first year, you know the word. It sits in the Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after the Creator and before without hate: nirbhau. Without fear. Yesterday's salok ended on it, after a whole universe of trembling: only the Formless is without fear. Today's salok, the next one in the var, starts there and refuses to move on quickly. Nanak, it says, the Formless is fearless. Then it looks at everything else people admire.
screen: `NIRBHAU, FROM THE MOOL MANTAR.` → `A UNIVERSE OF TREMBLING.` → `ONLY ONE WITHOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Two words carry this salok on ang 464. Nirbhau: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe we met yesterday. And nirankar: nir again, without, and akar, form or shape. The Formless. Together they answer a very human question: is there anything that isn't afraid? Everything else, yesterday's salok said, lives in awe. And anything with a form can break; it can be lost. The salok goes on to list what people admire and tell stories about, and sets each beside the Formless. So many celebrated figures are like dust. So many tales are told and retold, so many learned arguments made. People dance and sing for a crowd. Others wear earrings and necklaces worth a fortune, and the bodies that wear them, the salok says plainly, turn to ash. Then a turn worth noticing. Real wisdom isn't found through talk. Speaking of the One is as hard as iron. It comes by grace; cleverness and display only wear a person out. Here's why it matters. So much fear attaches to forms: a body getting sick, a job disappearing, a reputation cracking, a person leaving. The salok doesn't call those fears silly. Forms really do pass. What it offers is a place to stand. If only the Formless is fearless, then the way through fear, in Sikh teaching, isn't to become hard and fearless yourself. It's to stay close to the One who is. Some Sikh teachers put it in a short phrase: the one who fears the One fears nothing else.

segments.voice: Let one real fear come to mind, not the biggest, and notice the form it clings to: your health, your money, a person. Set it beside the whole sky, the wind and rivers moving in their order, and watch it take its true size; you don't have to make it disappear. If you pray, say nirbhau, nirankar, quietly.

545.title: The contented served
545.hook: those who served in contentment and meditated on truth were accepted (Asa di Var, ang 466)
545.howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara kitchen, cleaning, and serving the community, and this pauri of Asa di Var describes the contented spirit behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirbhau: only the Formless is fearless. Today, a pauri about the people who lived close to that One.

Visit a big gurdwara kitchen early in the morning. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. Someone is rolling rotis at a speed that looks impossible. An old man is stacking steel plates. Nobody is checking a clock, and nobody is waiting for thanks. Ask one of them why they're there, and they might just shrug and hand you a ball of dough. Guru Nanak described people like this in a single pauri, and it turns on one word.
screen: `A GURDWARA KITCHEN AT DAWN.` → `NOBODY WAITING FOR THANKS.` → `GURU NANAK'S ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The pauri is on ang 466, and it opens like this, in paraphrase: those who served were the contented ones, the ones who meditated on truth and nothing but truth. The word is santokh. Contentment. You've met it before on this path: Japji calls contentment one of the earrings of the true yogi. Here, it's what makes service real. Then the pauri describes these people. They did not set their foot on the path of wrong. They did good and lived by dharam, by righteousness. They broke the world's chains, and they ate and drank only a little. Then it turns to the One: you are the great giver, always giving more. By greatness, the Great One is found. So why contentment, of all things? Think about what discontent does to service. Serve hoping to be noticed, and every unnoticed hour stings. Serve to get something back, and you're keeping score. Serve while wishing you were somewhere else, and the work feels heavy, and so do you. Contentment takes all of that out. It doesn't mean wanting nothing for the world. It means being at peace with your own share while you work for others. Eating a little is part of the picture: not needing much leaves room for giving. In Sikh life, seva, selfless service, is everywhere: in the langar, in cleaning shoes, in sweeping the floor. This pauri gives seva its inner side. The hands serve. The heart is content. And the pauri says the ones who served that way were accepted.

segments.voice: Pick one small service you could do soon, washing a few dishes, refilling someone's water, and breathe out any wish to be noticed. Picture yourself doing it fully, finishing, and walking away without needing anyone to see, and feel what that's like in your chest. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Santokh, contentment: Guru Nanak's picture of true servants, content with little through santokh, rooted in truth, doing good without keeping score.
Your line: contented service. The hands serve; the heart is at peace. That's day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: What ego is
546.hook: this is ego: in ego we act, in ego we come and go; and the cure is within (Asa di Var M2, ang 466)
546.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on haumai in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching treats overcoming ego through the Guru's word as central to the spiritual life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, santokh: contented service, hands serving, heart at peace. Today, what gets in the way of all of it.
screen: `CONTENTED SERVICE.` · `A WEEK: WONDER, POWER, AWE, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: A compliment, and for a second a chest swells. Someone cuts in line, and a face goes hot. A correction in a meeting, and a whole afternoon goes to replaying it. Three moments, one center: me. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a salok on the same page of the Asa di Var as the contented servants. It reads like a doctor's notes. Here's the illness. Here's what it does. Here's where it comes from. And here, surprisingly, is where the medicine is kept.
screen: `PRAISE, INSULT, CORRECTION.` → `ONE CENTER: ME.` → `A DOCTOR'S NOTES FROM GURU ANGAD.`

segments.voice: The word is haumai. Hau means I, and mai is often read as me or mine, so haumai is something like I-me-ness: the self that keeps putting itself at the center. The salok, marked mahala 2 for Guru Angad, is on ang 466. In paraphrase: this is the nature of haumai. In haumai people do their deeds. This is haumai's bondage: again and again it brings people back into birth. Then Guru Angad asks two questions out loud. Where does haumai come from? And by what discipline does it leave? His answer to the first is honest and a little startling: haumai exists by the hukam, the divine order. It's part of how humans are made. People wander, he says, according to what they've done before. So ego isn't a shameful secret or a monster. It's a condition. Then the line that gives today its carry. Haumai is a deep, chronic illness. But the medicine is also within it. Daaroo bhee is maahi. The cure is in the same place as the disease. How? If the One gives grace, a person begins to live by the Guru's word, the shabad. And then, Nanak says, listen, people: by this discipline the pain goes. Elsewhere Gurbani speaks of overcoming haumai, even of killing it. This salok frames the work as healing, and names the medicine plainly: the Guru's word, lived, by grace. One way to hear it: the same self that sits at the center is the self the shabad turns toward the One.
screen: `HAUMAI: I-ME-NESS.` · `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` · `A CHRONIC ILLNESS.` · `THE MEDICINE IS WITHIN.` · then, large: `EGO, AND ITS CURE.`

segments.voice: Find one small moment from the last day where the I jumped to the center, a flash of pride, a sting, a need to be right, and watch it play again without judging. Notice where you felt it in your body; seeing isn't the cure, but it's where the turning can start. If you pray, say Waheguru, and let the moment go.
Haumai, I-me-ness: in Guru Angad's words, haumai is a chronic illness that keeps the self at the center, with its medicine found within.
Your line: ego, and its cure. The medicine is kept in the same place. See you tomorrow.
